meta.title: Theoretical Paradigms

blocks.x: An approach is a perspective involving certain beliefs about people and how they function. Several theories may exist within one approach, but they share common underlying assumptions. Multiple approaches exist because behaviour is determined by several different factors (biological, social, psychological).

Founded by Sigmund Freud (1856–1939). 'Psychodynamic' denotes the active forces within personality that motivate behaviour, including unconscious conflict between the structures that compose personality. The approach includes theories built on Freud's ideas by Jung, Adler, and Erikson.

blocks.name: Psychic <term d="The view that all behaviour has prior causes.">determinism</term>
blocks.def: The belief that all behaviour originates from childhood experiences residing in the unconscious.

items: Much of our behaviour is determined by unconscious thoughts and desires.
Maladaptive behaviour results from unresolved unconscious conflicts originating in childhood.
Resolution occurs through accessing and confronting those unresolved conflicts.

blocks.x: Freud's topography of mind: Conscious (here-and-now), Pre-conscious (easily retrievable memories), Unconscious (hard/impossible to retrieve). Psychoanalysis is a therapy that helps patients gain insight by exploring unconscious thoughts and emotions.

Freud's structural model: The id (unconscious, innate sexual/aggressive instincts, 'pleasure principle'), the ego ('reality principle', mediates between id and superego), and the superego (morals and rules of society, 'morality principle'). Conflicts among these cause anxiety, managed through ego defense mechanisms.

items: Repression — purposeful forgetting of anxiety-laden thoughts/memories/desires.
Displacement — expressing an unconscious impulse against a substitute target.
Projection — attributing one's own undesirable characteristics to others.
Reaction formation — an anxiety-laden impulse is replaced in consciousness by its opposite.
Denial — the ego fails to acknowledge threatening facts.
Regression — retreating to comforting behaviours of an earlier developmental stage during stress.

blocks.x: Criticisms: highly deterministic and reductionist; many concepts are unfalsifiable and lack scientific credibility; based on a small, unique sample (limited generalisability); too much emphasis on innate biological drives.

Neo-Freudians believed the ego had more control than the id, and considered social factors. Alfred Adler emphasized interpersonal/social factors and striving for superiority. Carl Jung emphasized the collective unconscious — inherited material from past generations, expressed through archetypes.
Proposed by J. B. Watson, with contributions from Pavlov, Skinner, and Thorndike. Behaviourists hold that all behaviour is learnt from the environment, to the neglect of innate/inherited factors.

items: <term d="The scientific study of behaviour and of the mental processes behind it.">Psychology</term> is the science of behaviour, not the mind.
Only observable behaviour should be studied.
Behaviour is determined by the environment.
All behaviour reduces to stimulus-response associations.
No reference is made to unobservable mental states.

blocks.name: <term d="Learning in which a neutral signal comes to trigger a reflex after being paired with something that naturally causes it.">Classical conditioning</term>
blocks.def: A <term d="A relatively permanent change in behaviour resulting from experience.">learning</term> process (Pavlov) whereby a neutral <term d="Any event or object that produces a response.">stimulus</term> comes to elicit a <term d="The reaction produced by a stimulus.">response</term> after being paired repeatedly with an <term d="A stimulus that naturally triggers a response without learning.">unconditioned stimulus</term> (UCS). Key terms: UCS (naturally evokes an unlearned response), UCR (the unlearned response), Neutral Stimulus (elicits no response), <term d="A previously neutral stimulus that triggers a response after pairing.">Conditioned Stimulus</term> (CS, previously neutral, now linked to UCS), <term d="A learned reaction to a previously neutral stimulus.">Conditioned Response</term> (CR, the learnt response to the CS).

blocks.x: Stimulus generalization — a CR occurs in weaker form to stimuli similar to (but different from) the original CS. Classical conditioning led to therapies like systematic desensitisation.

blocks.name: <term d="Learning in which behaviour is shaped by its consequences — reinforcement or punishment.">Operant conditioning</term>
blocks.def: First studied by Edward Thorndike (instrumental learning). Thorndike's law of effect: behaviours leading to reward increase in strength; those leading to punishment decrease in strength. Operates on reinforcement and punishment.

blocks.x: Bandura's theory — observational learning (learning through observation and imitation), vicarious learning, and modeling.

Evaluation: grossly oversimplified/mechanistic (ignores knowledge, motivation, subjective experience, emotion, innate factors, and cognition); reductionist (reduces complex behaviour to stimulus-response); deterministic (behaviour is seen as determined entirely by environment).
Called the 'third force' in psychology (emerged after behaviourist and psychodynamic approaches). Founded by Abraham Maslow, with Carl Rogers and Rollo May.

items: Rooted in existentialist thought — humans have <term d="The view that people can choose their own actions.">free will</term> and freedom of choice.

People are basically good and have an innate <term d="A state of deprivation that drives behaviour toward satisfying it.">need</term> to grow, develop, and achieve full potential (self-actualisation).
Subjective, conscious experience of the individual is of primary interest.
Humans must be understood in terms of their own subjective views, self-perceptions, and feelings of self-worth.

blocks.name: Maslow's <term d="Maslow's model arranging human needs from basic survival to self-actualization.">Hierarchy of Needs</term>
blocks.def: Psychopathology's primary cause is failure to gratify fundamental needs. Deficiency drives: Physiological, Safety, Love & belonging, Esteem needs. Growth drives: Cognitive, Aesthetic needs. Topped by Self-actualization needs.

items: Physiological needs — most basic (oxygen, water, protein, vitamins, minerals).
Safety needs — protection, stability, freedom from anxiety.
Love & belonging needs — friends, partner, community; unmet needs cause loneliness/social anxiety.
Esteem needs — respect, status, recognition (lower level); self-respect, confidence, achievement (higher level); unmet needs cause low self-worth.
Cognitive needs — understanding and knowledge. Aesthetic needs — order and beauty.
Self-actualisation — continuous desire to fulfil potential.

blocks.name: Rogers' Person-Centered Approach
blocks.def: Centered on the self-concept. If self-concept closely matches the ideal self, high self-esteem results; a large mismatch causes psychological distress. Rogers believed people can solve their own problems given the right opportunity and support. Core conditions for therapeutic change: empathy, unconditional positive regard, and congruence/genuineness.

blocks.x: Evaluation: not a single comprehensive theory, but a collection of diverse theories; difficult to test empirically; Rogers' three core conditions are arguably just what good counsellors/health professionals do anyway.

Concerned with human thought processes and how they interact with behaviour — <term d="The processes by which information is encoded, stored and retrieved.">memory</term>, learning, intelligence, thinking, and language. Unlike other approaches, cognitive theory has no single unifying theory and no one central founder.

items: Acknowledges unobservable mental processes and their importance in determining/predicting behaviour.
Accepts empiricist ideas and the scientific method; based mainly on laboratory experiments.
Views the mind as an information processor — computing answers to problems analogous to a computer.

blocks.name: Information processing approach
blocks.def: The mind is analogous to a system that inputs, stores, and retrieves data, used flexibly across cognitive tasks. Sequence: Stimulus → <term d="The focusing of mental resources on selected information.">Attention</term> → <term d="The process of organising and interpreting sensory information.">Perception</term> → Thought Processes → Decision → Response.

blocks.name: <term d="A mental framework that organises knowledge and guides interpretation.">Schema</term>
blocks.def: A cognitive structure containing knowledge about a thing, its attributes, and relations among attributes. It guides how individuals perceive and interpret events — the basic building block of cognitive processes.

blocks.x: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) combines both cognitive and behavioural principles.
Evaluation: much research is conducted in artificial laboratory environments; mechanistic; ignores social factors, emotion, and biology (e.g. hormones).
Biological theories focus on biological processes, and genes and their relationship to behaviour. Evaluation: ignores environmental and psychological factors in explaining behaviour.

The Biopsychosocial(s) Model integrates biological factors, psychological factors, and social factors in explaining behaviour, with consideration of a spiritual component — offering a more holistic alternative to any single approach above.

mnemonics.h: SLC — three cues for abnormal behaviour
lines: Statistical infrequency, personal distress, and maladaptive/impaired functioning — the three go-to criteria for spotting abnormal behaviour.
Reinforcement always increases a behaviour; punishment always decreases it — regardless of whether something is added (positive) or removed (negative).
Antecedent, Behaviour, Consequence — the basic chain behaviourists analyse to explain why a behaviour keeps happening.

mnemonics.h: DEPC — the four goals of psychology
lines: Describe, Explain/understand, Predict, Control — the four things every psychological study is ultimately trying to do.

id (Pleasure), ego (reality — 'I'), superego (morality — think '<term d="The moral principles governing how research and practice should be conducted.">Ethics</term>') — the three parts constantly negotiating behaviour.
Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules (like gambling) are the hardest to extinguish — Very Resistant to stopping.
